analysis.one_liner: Moves the U.S. to 100% clean energy by 2050, using a carbon fee returned to households as dividends.
analysis.headline: A sweeping Democratic climate bill with household dividends and worker transition aid never got a hearing or a vote, dying in the Senate Finance Committee when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This was Senator Jeff Merkley's comprehensive climate bill: it aimed to get the United States onto 100% clean energy by 2050, put a fee on carbon pollution, and send that money back to households while funding retraining and income support for energy workers whose jobs would change, plus targeted help for low-income and disadvantaged communities [S3]. It also proposed clean-energy bonds whose proceeds would go into a dedicated Climate Fund to pay for the transition [S2]. It was introduced in April 2017, read twice, and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance — and that is where the record ends [S1] [S5]. No hearing, no amendment, no vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2019 [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday households, who would receive a dividend from the carbon pollution fee that refunds energy costs back to people [S3]. Workers in coal, oil, and gas jobs, who would get retraining, transition assistance, and temporary unemployment support [S3]. Low-income, disadvantaged, and energy-burdened communities, which the bill singles out for targeted funding and consumer protections [S3]. Renewable energy and clean-technology businesses, which would gain from the buildout and from a Climate Fund financed by clean-energy bond proceeds [S2]. Future generations, in the bill's stated purpose of avoiding the most dangerous impacts of climate change [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill set a national goal of reaching 100% clean energy by 2050 to avoid the most dangerous impacts of climate change, which would mean less fossil-fuel air pollution affecting public health.

It included retraining, transition support, and temporary additional unemployment compensation for workers whose fossil-energy jobs were phased out, plus direct assistance tied to worker benefit plans.
It directed specific funding and consumer protections toward disadvantaged and low-income communities, including community development organizations for efficiency and climate mitigation projects.
It authorized clean-energy bonds whose proceeds had to be deposited into a dedicated Climate Fund used to carry out the bill's programs.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal producers, who would pay a rising fee on the carbon content of their products and see demand for their main product phased down over decades [S3]. Fossil-heavy industries and utilities, which would have to replace fossil generation and infrastructure. Energy consumers would face higher fossil prices, though the bill returns fee revenue to households as dividends and shields low-income communities [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, gas, and coal producers first.

drawbacks.text: A carbon fee raises the price of gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity from fossil sources before dividends flow, and critics could reasonably question whether every household — especially energy-heavy and rural ones — would be made whole; the bill text itself includes consumer-protection provisions, an acknowledgment of this risk.

Reaching 100% clean energy by 2050 is a fifteen-year overhaul of the entire energy system; the transition costs, and whether retraining and unemployment support for displaced energy workers are adequate, are the main costs an honest supporter would concede.
The bill drew no Republican support and was never negotiated in committee, so its design was never tested against amendment or compromise before it died.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is progressive on its face: a carbon fee's cost falls heaviest on fossil producers and heavy fossil users, while most revenue returns to households as dividends and workers in declining industries get retraining and income support [S3]. The real costs are borne by fossil-fuel companies and fossil-dependent regions, plus the execution risk of any 15-year system-wide transition. The bill was broad and un-negotiated, so cost estimates and offsets were never refined in committee. The largest cost in what actually happened falls on ordinary people, who got none of the bill's benefits: no dividend, no transition aid, and continued reliance on fossil energy.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on April 27, 2017 and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Finance.
No further action was ever taken on it — the committee never held a hearing or markup, and the full Senate never voted.
The bill carried 4 cosponsors alongside its sponsor and died when the 115th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil-fuel producers and utilities that continue business as usual: no carbon fee, no 100% clean-energy mandate, and no transition funding ever took effect. The status quo on climate, energy prices, and pollution stayed exactly as it was.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil-fuel producers and the status quo.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate and became its only active sponsor when it was referred to committee.

for.name: Four Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a total of five Senate supporters.

against.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; no hearing or markup on the bill was ever held during his tenure in the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The fight never reached a floor vote, but the dividing line was purely partisan: the sponsor and all 4 cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican supported or acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill's core mechanism is a fee on carbon pollution, which directly raises the cost of producing and selling fossil fuels and phases down demand for their main product; industry interests run against the bill's health and climate benefits for the public.

A 100% clean-energy target plus a bond-financed Climate Fund and community efficiency programs would channel large new investment into clean power and efficiency — growth that rides alongside the public benefits the bill is designed to deliver.

Utilities would face pressure to replace fossil generation, risking stranded assets in coal and gas plants, while the bill's buildout and financing create new demand and investment opportunities for the same utilities.
